patient.chief_complaint: Grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy with melena and hemodynamic compromise
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. R. is a 61-year-old Hispanic man with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 26) and prior grade III esophageal varices who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for progressive confusion and black tarry stools over the past 24 hours. The wife reports he was increasingly confused yesterday afternoon, could not recognize their grandchildren at dinner, and by this morning could not state his own name. She found bloody-appearing black stool in the toilet bowl multiple times. He has been drinking alcohol daily despite medical advice — wife confirms he drank yesterday. On arrival he is hemodynamically compromised with blood pressure 98/58, heart rate 122, and pale conjunctiva. His wife explains that he has been on lactulose and rifaximin for secondary HE prophylaxis following an episode 8 months ago. His rectal exam reveals melena confirming active upper GI bleeding, which in the setting of known grade III varices likely represents variceal hemorrhage. The combination of active GI bleed and advanced cirrhosis has resulted in massive nitrogen load to the gut (blood protein digestion → ammonia), precipitating the current acute hepatic encephalopathy episode. Ammonia is 194 µmol/L — markedly elevated. He also continues metformin despite cirrhosis, which represents a prescribing concern given lactic acidosis risk in hepatic impairment.

Chronic bilateral basal ganglia hypodensity — hepatocerebral degeneration in cirrhosis. Structural cause of encephalopathy excluded.

output.indication: Active GI hemorrhage, melena, known varices — evaluate source and treat

findings.description: Active oozing from grade III esophageal varices at 30-35 cm from incisors. Three bands placed with successful hemostasis. Gastric varices fundus — small, not actively bleeding. No peptic ulcer disease. No portal hypertensive gastropathy bleeding.

output.result: Grade III esophageal variceal hemorrhage — band ligation performed with hemostasis achieved. Three varices banded.
output.impression: Active variceal hemorrhage as source of GI bleed. Band ligation successful. Start octreotide infusion. IV ceftriaxone prophylaxis (SBP/bacteremia prophylaxis post-variceal bleed — standard of care). Repeat endoscopy in 1-2 weeks.
recommendations: Continue octreotide 50 mcg/h IV for 2-5 days
IV ceftriaxone 1g daily x7 days (antibiotic prophylaxis after variceal bleed)
STOP metformin permanently (contraindicated in cirrhosis — lactic acidosis)
Restart propranolol after hemostasis achieved and hemodynamics stable

critical_actions: Administer IV thiamine 500 mg BEFORE any glucose — Wernicke prophylaxis mandatory in alcoholic cirrhosis
Urgent endoscopy for variceal hemorrhage — primary precipitant identification and treatment
Lactulose titrated to 2-3 stools/day (NOT maximum diarrhea — excessive diarrhea causes hypokalemia and paradoxical HE)
IV ceftriaxone prophylaxis post-variceal bleed (reduces bacteremia/SBP and 5-day mortality)
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude concurrent SBP
STOP metformin permanently — contraindicated in hepatic impairment (lactic acidosis risk)
STOP propranolol during acute hemorrhage — worsens hypotension; restart after hemodynamic stability
Transplant evaluation referral — MELD-Na 26 with two overt HE episodes
contraindicated_actions: Flumazenil or naloxone as primary treatment: No benzodiazepine or opiate on toxicology screen — reversal agents not indicated
Continue metformin: Metformin contraindicated in hepatic impairment — lactic acidosis risk confirmed by lactate 4.8
Administer dextrose before thiamine: Risk precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in thiamine-deficient alcoholic
Avoid antibiotics post-variceal hemorrhage: Antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone) post-variceal bleed is standard of care — failure to give increases 5-day mortality
Restrict propranolol during acute hemorrhage: Beta-blockade during hemodynamic compromise worsens hypotension — hold until hemostasis
teaching_pearls: BUN elevation out of proportion to creatinine (BUN:Cr >20) points to upper GI hemorrhage as ammonia source — a single lab ratio confirms the precipitant
Metformin in cirrhosis causes lactic acidosis — always review medications for contraindications in liver disease
Propranolol is life-saving for varices prophylaxis but must be held during active hemorrhage (hypotension risk)
Post-variceal hemorrhage antibiotic prophylaxis reduces 5-day mortality — do not omit ceftriaxone
Restrictive transfusion (Hgb target ≥7) reduces portal pressure and rebleeding risk in cirrhotic GI hemorrhage — overtransfusion worsens portal hypertension
key_reasoning_points: GI hemorrhage is the classic HE precipitant — blood in gut provides massive nitrogen load (blood protein digested to ammonia by gut bacteria); BUN:Cr ratio >20 is the biochemical signature of upper GI bleed
EEG triphasic waves with anterior-to-posterior phase lag are pathognomonic of metabolic encephalopathy (HE) — no epileptiform discharges excludes NCSE
Thiamine must precede glucose in any alcoholic patient — Wernicke prophylaxis
Metformin is contraindicated in hepatic impairment — causes lactic acidosis; lactate 4.8 on this case is a teaching point
Antibiotic prophylaxis after variceal hemorrhage is not optional — ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone for 7 days reduces bacteremia, SBP, and 5-day mortality (RCT evidence)
Propranolol worsens hemorrhagic shock — hold beta-blockers during acute GI bleeding in cirrhotics
Lactulose target is 2-3 stools/day — exceeding this causes hypokalemia and electrolyte-driven paradoxical HE
MELD-Na 26 with two overt HE episodes — AASLD transplant evaluation threshold met; refer urgently
